That works out to about $1,380 a month for maintenance, property taxes and homeowners insurance. The figures come from the Zillow and Thumbtack release of October 22, 2026. Maintenance makes up about two-thirds of that total. The hidden cost of owning a home calculator below starts with those national typical amounts. Replace them with your own tax bill, insurance quote and maintenance reserve to see what owning costs you each month, each year and over five years. In our internal cost modeling, we ran a newer home that needs $3,000 a year of maintenance through the calculator. It keeps the typical $3,129 property tax bill and $2,266 insurance premium. Its hidden cost comes to $8,395 a year, or $699.58 a month. That is $8,171 a year below the national typical. Over five years at 3% yearly growth, the total is $44,570. Replace them with your own numbers. Cost of owning on top of the mortgage, per month $1,381 Your maintenance, tax and insurance total matches the typical U.S. homeowner. Per year $16,566 Set aside for maintenance, per month $931 Total over 5 years $87,951 Year 5 at 3% growth $18,645 Maintenance 67%, property taxes 19%, insurance 14% of the yearly total. Estimate only. The starting figures are national typical amounts reported from the 2026 Zillow and Thumbtack study, not a quote for any house. Utilities, furnishings, remodeling you choose to do, mortgage insurance and income-tax effects of owning are not included. How it works The calculator adds three yearly costs and one monthly cost: maintenance and repairs, property taxes, homeowners insurance and homeowners association (HOA) dues. Its starting values are the national typical amounts from the Zillow and Thumbtack study: $11,171 for maintenance, $3,129 for property taxes and $2,266 for insurance. Those add to $16,566 a year, or $1,380.50 a month on top of the mortgage. These starting values are typical amounts reported for the whole country. They are not a quote for any house. In our internal cost modeling, we ran the calculator's arithmetic over seven homeowner scenarios, including a low-maintenance home, a condo with HOA dues and a high-insurance market. We chose those scenarios ourselves to see how far one household's cost can sit from the national typical. None of them was measured on a real house or drawn from a client case, and you can enter the same numbers in the calculator above to check them. With the national inputs, maintenance alone is $930.92 a month. Maintenance takes 67% of the total, property taxes 19% and insurance 14%. With nothing entered, the calculator returns $0 and asks for the three yearly figures. Maintenance, property taxes and insurance sit on separate lines because you find each number in a different place. Your property tax figure is the yearly amount on your tax bill. The calculator leaves out the income-tax effects of owning, and our tax deductions for homeowners guide covers that side of property taxes. Your insurance figure is the yearly premium on a homeowners insurance quote. Maintenance has no bill, so you enter a yearly reserve for upkeep and repairs. In the study, Thumbtack built the maintenance figure from home projects requested on Thumbtack, and Zillow estimated property taxes and insurance for a typical U.S. homeowner. If your home has HOA dues, enter the monthly amount and the calculator multiplies it by 12. The calculator projects your costs forward with a simple growth rule. Year one is your yearly total. Each later year is the previous year times one plus the growth rate, and the projection total is the sum of the years. The default growth rate is 3%. In the study, overall costs rose 2.8% over the last year, which rounds to about 3%. At the national inputs, five years at 3% growth total $87,951. The fifth year alone comes to $18,645. With no growth over ten years, the total is $165,660. Maintenance growth slowed to 1% in 2026. It had been 9% in 2022. The national typical can sit far from one household's real cost, and three of our modeled cases show how far. A low-maintenance home with $3,000 of yearly upkeep and the typical tax and insurance figures costs $8,395 a year. That is $699.58 a month, or $8,171 below the national typical. Our condo case uses $3,000 for maintenance, $3,129 for property taxes and $800 for insurance. Those three lines add to $6,929, which is $9,637 below the national typical. Add $400 a month of HOA dues, or $4,800 a year, and the household total is $11,729. That is $977.42 a month, and HOA dues make up 41% of it. The comparison line in the calculator leaves HOA out, so it shows the $9,637 gap. Compare the full $11,729 total against the national $16,566 as a separate step. A high-insurance market moves the cost the other way, and the release puts Miami insurance at nearly $5,000 a year. Put $5,000 of insurance into the national inputs and the total becomes $19,300 a year. That is $1,608.33 a month and $2,734 above the national typical. Its five-year total is $102,466. Over five years, the national total in the study is up 31.7%. Insurance rose fastest, up 54%. Maintenance is up 32% and property taxes are up 19% over the same period. Those changes describe what already happened. They do not predict the next five years, so the growth rate stays an input you can edit. If your own insurance quotes have climbed faster than your other costs, raise the growth rate to see a more cautious projection. The mortgage line is optional. Enter your monthly principal and interest to see mortgage plus these costs per month, and enter a home value to see the yearly cost as a percent of that value. With the national inputs, a $2,200 payment and a $400,000 home, the all-in cost is $3,580.50 a month. The yearly cost on top of the mortgage is 4.1% of that home value. The $2,200 payment and $400,000 value are illustrative inputs we picked. To size the mortgage itself, use our home affordability calculator . If you are deciding between renting and buying, the rent vs buy calculator shows the break-even year. The calculator leaves out utilities, furnishings, remodeling you choose to do, mortgage insurance and the income-tax effects of owning. The study covers the typical U.S. homeowner and 30 metro areas, and costs vary by market. The release does not define a typical home or state the home value behind the typical figures. Across the metros, the total ranges from $14,187 in Phoenix to $25,111 in New York. Six metros top $3,000 a year for insurance. The low-maintenance, condo, high-insurance and mortgage cases above are our own illustrative inputs. They describe no real house. Treat $1,380 a month as the national typical starting point. Then replace it with your own insurance quote, property tax bill and maintenance reserve, and budget the sum. In our internal cost modeling, a newer home or a condo whose association pays for exteriors ran well below the typical, as the $3,000-maintenance case at $8,395 a year shows. A high-premium market can run well above it, as the $5,000-insurance case at $19,300 a year shows. Your own quotes change the answer. If you already have a full year of your own bills, use those totals directly. If you are weighing renting against buying, the rent vs buy calculator fits that decision better. This calculator gives educational estimates and is not financial advice. If you are shopping for a home, add your three quotes to our home buying checklist so the hidden cost of owning a home is in your budget from the first month. Frequently asked questions How much does it cost to own a home each year beyond the mortgage? The typical homeowner pays $16,566 a year beyond the mortgage, which is $1,380.50 a month. That figure covers maintenance, property taxes and homeowners insurance in the Zillow and Thumbtack study. Your own number depends on your insurance quote, tax bill and maintenance reserve, which you can enter in the calculator above. What are the hidden costs of owning a home? The study names maintenance at $11,171 a year, property taxes at $3,129 and homeowners insurance at $2,266. Maintenance is the largest, at about two-thirds of the total. Some homes also carry HOA dues, which the calculator takes as a monthly amount. How much should I budget for home maintenance each month? The national typical maintenance figure works out to $930.92 a month. In our low-maintenance case, with $3,000 a year of upkeep, the set-aside drops to $250 a month. Enter your own yearly reserve, and the calculator shows the monthly set-aside. Which hidden cost of homeownership has risen fastest? Homeowners insurance has risen fastest, up 54% over five years. Maintenance is up 32% and property taxes are up 19% over the same period. Miami has the highest insurance cost in the study, at nearly $5,000 a year. Does this calculator include the mortgage payment? No, the headline figure is the cost on top of the mortgage. If you enter your monthly principal and interest, the calculator adds a line showing mortgage plus these costs per month. With a home value entered, it also shows the yearly cost as a percent of that value. Why might my cost be lower than the national typical? Your cost sits below the typical when your upkeep or insurance runs lower. A home with $3,000 of yearly maintenance comes to $8,395 a year, which is $8,171 below the national typical. Our condo case, with $3,000 maintenance and $800 insurance, totals $6,929 on the three lines. Its $4,800 of yearly HOA dues lift the household total to $11,729. How much will these costs grow over five years? At the default 3% yearly growth, the national typical reaches $18,645 in the fifth year. The five-year total is $87,951. The 3% matches the reported one-year change of 2.8%, rounded, and works as a planning default. Change the growth rate to test a faster or slower rise. What does this calculator leave out? It leaves out utilities, furnishings, remodeling you choose to do, mortgage insurance and the income-tax effects of owning. It also leaves out the mortgage payment unless you enter it. Budget those costs separately from the calculator's total. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. It also lowers the market value of bonds you already own. At ModernWallet, we see savers rethink their fed rate hike savings and investments strategy the moment a policy meeting concludes. When the central bank raises interest rates, the financial effects split in two directions: new yields rise, but existing fixed-rate securities drop in resale value. Your time horizon determines whether to act or hold steady. Tools for this journey High-yield savings calculator → What the October 2026 Fed Hold Means for Savings, CDs and Mortgages The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) held the federal funds target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent on October 28, 2026. That hold changes no rate you already have. The Federal Reserve's statement reports a 10 to 2 vote. Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack dissented because they preferred a 1/4 percentage point increase at this meeting. The statement says "Inflation remains elevated" and describes economic activity as expanding at a strong pace, with the unemployment rate little changed. A certificate of deposit (CD) you already opened keeps its rate for the full term, as the CD section below explains. Each bank sets its own rates on new CDs and savings accounts. Enter a bank's quote in the CD calculator or read the high-yield savings account (HYSA) vs CD comparison before you pick one. The two dissenting votes are not a decision, and the target range stayed where the September 16 hike put it. A fixed-rate loan you already have is unaffected by the hold. Freddie Mac's weekly survey put the average 30-year fixed rate at 7.24% on October 29, down from 7.32% a week earlier. Freddie Mac builds that average from rates offered Thursday through Wednesday, so the figure ends on October 28, the day of the decision, and cannot show how lenders reacted to it. Your own quote can differ, so compare it using the mortgage rates guide . The statement gives no explicit guidance about the next meeting. If you hold bonds, the sections below explain how a rate change affects their price. Before you lock a CD term, compare current bank quotes. Then read the Federal Reserve statement after the December 8-9, 2026 meeting , which comes with a Summary of Economic Projections. The Federal Funds Rate Mechanism and Borrowing Costs The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) sets a target range for the federal funds rate at eight scheduled meetings each year. This benchmark governs the interest rate commercial banks charge one another for overnight loans. While the central bank does not set retail loan rates directly, adjustments to this benchmark ripple quickly through the broader financial system. When the policy rate rises, banks face higher costs for short-term liquidity. Lenders pass those expenses to borrowers by lifting the prime rate and short-term indices tied to consumer debt. According to the Federal Reserve , these higher financing costs help cool economic activity by making borrowing more expensive across the economy. The immediate impact lands on variable-rate credit cards, home equity lines of credit (HELOCs), and newly issued auto loans. Mortgage rates also respond to broader monetary policy and inflation expectations, as detailed in our guide on current mortgage rates . Higher rates increase monthly debt service for households carrying revolving balances. The September 2026 Rate Increase in Practice On September 16, 2026, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raised the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3-3/4 to 4 percent. Even after that increase, the 0.38 percent average sits well below the 3.7 percent CPI.The unanimous 12-0 vote marked the central bank's first rate increase since 2023. The Federal Reserve's official policy statement stated the decision supports a return to its 2 percent inflation target, while updated projections signaled another potential rate hike in 2026. A 25-basis-point hike lifts cash returns modestly. For example, an illustrative $10,000 deposit receiving the full 0.25 percentage point rise in annual percentage yield (APY) generates an additional $25 in interest over one year. Because retail institutions rarely pass through the complete hike, calculate realistic returns on your balance with our high-yield savings calculator . Borrowing costs react much faster when benchmark rates climb. For example, an illustrative $20,000 variable home equity line of credit (HELOC) balance incurs $50 in extra annual interest after a full 25-basis-point adjustment. Existing fixed loans remain insulated from these rate moves, as detailed in our mortgage rates guide . Existing Bond Prices and the Maturity Distinction An interest rate hike reduces the market price of bonds you already own if you sell them before maturity. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions. As the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) notes, when prevailing interest rates rise, existing bonds paying lower fixed coupon rates become less attractive to secondary-market buyers. Consider a concrete example. Suppose you own a $1,000 bond paying a fixed 3% coupon, which delivers $30 in annual interest. If the central bank raises rates and comparable newly issued bonds pay 5% ($50 annually), no buyer will pay $1,000 for your 3% bond. To attract a buyer, your bond's resale price must fall until its total return matches the prevailing 5% market yield. That decline represents a paper loss on your brokerage statement. This drop in resale value only affects you if you liquidate the position early. If you hold an individual bond to maturity, you still receive your promised interest payments and full principal repayment, assuming the issuer does not default. The rate hike changes its interim market quote, not its contractual cash flow. However, duration risk influences how far that interim price falls. Bonds with longer maturities carry higher duration risk because their fixed payments remain locked below market rates for more years. A 20-year bond drops substantially more in price than a 2-year note during a rate shock. Shorter-duration debt protects capital better when rates climb. New Debt Purchases and Bond Yield Timing A Federal Reserve rate hike increases the yields available on newly issued fixed-income securities. Issuers of corporate debt, municipal bonds, and government obligations must offer higher payouts to compete with prevailing market rates. According to TreasuryDirect , newly auctioned Treasury bills, notes, and bonds reflect these higher benchmark rates directly at auction. For investors with unallocated cash, higher coupon rates present a stronger income stream than was available before the rate adjustment. Locking in a higher yield today provides guaranteed cash flow for the life of the security. Yet yield timing carries an inherent tradeoff. If the central bank raises rates multiple times, debt purchased today will see its market value decline as subsequent issues offer even higher yields. Conversely, waiting for peak rates risks leaving cash in lower-yielding instruments if the central bank pauses or reverses course sooner than expected. Savers evaluating newly issued fixed-income options often compare certificates of deposit (CDs) against short-term government debt, a tradeoff we examine in our CD vs. Treasury bill comparison. Fed Rate Hike Savings and Investments in Cash Deposits Commercial bank deposit rates tend to rise after a policy hike, but they rarely match the Federal Reserve's rate change in size or speed. The central bank does not set retail deposit rates. As the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) explains, individual banks establish their own savings and money market interest rates based on their balance-sheet needs and funding requirements. Online banks and high-yield institutions generally raise yields faster than traditional brick-and-mortar lenders to attract customer deposits. Even then, deposit pass-through remains well below 100%. Savers comparing flexible cash options can review our HYSA vs. money market account breakdown or run projections using our high-yield savings calculator . Certificates of deposit introduce a different timing dynamic because they lock in a fixed yield for a specified period. Opening a CD immediately before a hike locks your capital into a lower pre-hike rate for the entire term. Waiting until after the hike allows you to capture the higher return for the duration of the agreement. The tradeoff balances rate certainty against opportunity cost. A locked CD guarantees your return if rates tumble, but it leaves you behind if the central bank continues tightening. Our guide comparing a HYSA vs. CD details how to weigh this flexibility against guaranteed term yields. Federal Reserve Projections and Rate Paths Financial markets evaluate whether a rate hike is an isolated event or the start of an extended tightening cycle by studying central bank projections. Every quarter, the Federal Open Market Committee publishes its Summary of Economic Projections . This release includes the dot plot, which visualizes where each committee member expects the federal funds rate to settle over the coming years. The dot plot serves as a gauge of policy sentiment rather than a formal guarantee. Policymakers do not pre-commit to future rate moves. Instead, the committee adjusts policy meeting by meeting based on incoming data on inflation, employment, and economic output. When the dot plot indicates several additional hikes ahead, fixed-income yields across all maturities often adjust upward before those meetings even occur. If projections point toward a pause, bond markets tend to stabilize. Monitoring these official forecasts helps investors avoid assuming that a single rate increase will immediately be followed by another. Equity Valuations and the Discount Rate A Federal Reserve rate hike exerts downward valuation pressure on stocks by increasing the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings. Equity valuation models calculate the present value of a business by discounting its projected future cash flows back to today's dollars. When interest rates rise, that mathematical discount factor increases, reducing the calculated present worth of distant profits. This discount mechanism affects fast-growing companies particularly hard because much of their expected profit sits years in the future. Higher yields on cash and government bonds also provide investors with viable alternatives to equities. Capital that previously pursued stock market returns can find acceptable yields in safer debt instruments. Rate increases can also cause stocks and bonds to decline simultaneously. While balanced portfolios rely on bonds to cushion equity declines, an inflation shock can depress both asset classes together. We examine this shifting relationship in our guide on stocks vs. bonds . Who Should Not Reallocate After a Policy Shift Investors with long-term horizons who hold individual bonds to maturity should not alter their asset allocation in response to a rate hike. If your objective is predictable income and capital preservation at redemption, interim secondary-market price fluctuations do not diminish your final payout. Selling seasoned bonds at a paper loss to chase slightly higher yields on new issues incurs transaction costs and locks in an otherwise temporary decline. Similarly, systematic equity index investors should avoid shifting into cash. Attempting to time interest rate cycles requires predicting both policy moves and market reactions. Investors with time horizons exceeding seven years should maintain their existing contribution schedules rather than reacting to short-term Federal Reserve headlines. Conditions That Would Change This Guidance Our perspective on portfolio positioning would change if economic indicators trigger a rapid shift toward monetary easing. If inflation slows abruptly and unemployment rises, the Federal Open Market Committee could pause hikes or cut rates. Under those conditions, the yield advantage on cash and short-term paper would vanish quickly. In an easing environment, longer-duration bonds would gain strong capital appreciation as their fixed payments become more valuable. A shift in your personal timeline would also alter this advice. If you transition from accumulating wealth to needing immediate liquidity for a home purchase, prioritizing capital preservation in insured cash accounts outweighs long-term asset positioning. Action Steps for Fed Rate Hike Savings and Investments You can optimize your portfolio after a policy adjustment by auditing your cash yields and reviewing the duration of your debt holdings. Begin by verifying the current annual percentage yield (APY) on your primary savings account. If your bank has not adjusted its rates upward, transfer surplus emergency reserves to a competitive high-yield account or short-term Treasury bills. Next, review the average duration of any bond mutual funds or exchange-traded funds (ETFs) in your portfolio. Confirm that your fixed-income allocation aligns with your tolerance for short-term price volatility. Check your bank's latest rate schedule and the Federal Reserve's policy calendar before making any final portfolio changes to your fed rate hike savings and investments. Frequently asked questions What does a Fed rate hike mean for my savings account? It usually raises the annual percentage yield (APY) on your savings account. Commercial banks set their own rates independently. Because of that flexibility, institutions adjust yields at varying speeds and rarely match the full Federal Reserve rate move. Does a Fed rate hike hurt bonds I already own? It hurts their resale price if you sell before maturity. New debt arrives with higher coupons, which makes older, lower-paying bonds less attractive to secondary-market buyers. If you hold a bond to its maturity date, you still receive all scheduled coupon payments and your full principal back. Is now a good time to buy bonds? It can be an attractive entry point for newly issued debt. New issues pay higher coupons than older issues. However, if the central bank raises rates again later, market prices on those new purchases will drop temporarily. Will a Fed rate hike raise my CD rate? A rate hike will not change the yield on a certificate of deposit (CD) you already opened. The rate is locked for the entire term. New certificates of deposit issued after the hike, however, will generally offer higher fixed yields than older issues. How does a Fed rate hike affect the stock market? Higher interest rates often create headwinds for equity valuations. They increase the discount rate analysts apply to future corporate earnings, which depresses the present value of those cash flows. Rising yields on cash and bonds also create stiffer competition for investor dollars. How do I know if the Fed will keep raising rates? You cannot know with certainty. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) publishes its Summary of Economic Projections quarterly, which contains the dot plot showing member rate forecasts. The central bank evaluates economic data before each meeting and never guarantees future rate adjustments in advance. That year depends on your mortgage rate, your rent, how fast the home gains value and what your invested cash earns. The defaults are a $400,000 home, $2,200 monthly rent and a 7.32% mortgage rate. With those inputs, the modeled break-even is year 21, and a 5% rate moves it to year 5. The rent vs buy calculator below compares your net worth if you buy with your net worth if you rent and invest the same cash. It also shows the year buying pulls ahead. In our internal modeling, we took a buyer who puts 20% down on the default $400,000 home and pays 3% in closing costs. That is $92,000 of cash on day one and a $320,000 loan. At 7.32% over 30 years, the principal and interest payment is $2,198.18 a month. Adding property tax, insurance and maintenance brings the first-month cost of owning to $3,032. A similar rental costs $2,215 a month with renter's insurance. The renter invests the $92,000 and the $817 monthly difference at a 6% return. Seven years in, buying leaves $169,338 and renting and investing leaves $210,495, so renting leads by $41,156. Everything else is a planning assumption you can change. Property tax and insurance vary a lot by state. After 7 years, renting is ahead by $41,156 Renting ends $41,156 ahead after 7 years. Buying only passes renting in year 21. Net worth if you buy $169,338 Net worth if you rent and invest $210,495 Break-even year Year 21 Mortgage payment (principal and interest) $2,198 First-month cost of owning $3,032 First-month cost of renting $2,215 Cash needed to buy $92,000 Price-to-rent ratio 15.2 Year Buy Rent and invest Buy minus rent 1 $70,335 $107,585 -$37,249 3 $100,743 $140,054 -$39,311 5 $133,658 $174,328 -$40,669 7 $169,338 $210,495 -$41,156 10 $228,681 $268,496 -$39,815 15 $346,033 $375,959 -$29,926 20 $498,137 $503,958 -$5,821 30 $1,021,427 $902,512 $118,915 Estimate only. Modeled results, not a forecast of home prices, rents or investment returns. Net worth counts the home's value after selling costs minus the loan, plus whatever each path invests. It leaves out income-tax effects of owning (mortgage interest and property tax only help if you itemize), moving costs, and special assessments. How it works The calculator tracks two paths, buying and renting, month by month. Buying costs the down payment and closing costs on day one. Each month after that, the buyer pays the mortgage payment plus property tax, insurance and maintenance, each figured as a percent of the home's current value. HOA dues are added, and so is mortgage insurance at 0.5% of the original loan a year. Mortgage insurance applies only while the down payment is under 20% and the loan is above 80% of the price. Renting costs the rent, which grows each year, plus renter's insurance. The renter keeps the down payment and closing costs and invests them on day one. Each month, whichever path costs less invests the difference. At every year-end, buying net worth is the home value after selling costs, minus the loan balance, plus the buyer's own investments. Renting net worth is the renter's investments. The break-even year is the first year-end at which buying net worth is at least renting net worth. In our internal modeling, we compared buying with renting and investing the same cash over 1 to 30 years. We then changed one assumption at a time to see which ones move the break-even year. We wrote the model twice, once in Python and once in the calculator's TypeScript code, and the two versions agreed on every scenario below. You can enter the same numbers in the calculator above to check them. At the defaults, owning costs more than renting in the first month. The price-to-rent ratio, which is the price divided by 12 months of rent, is 15.2. Buying trails renting by $39,311 after 3 years. After 5 years, the gap is $40,669. After 7 years, it reaches $41,156. The gap then starts to close and is $39,815 after 10 years. After 15 years, buying is worth $346,033 and renting is worth $375,959. Renting is still ahead by $29,926 at that point. Buying first catches up in year 21, which is the break-even year at the defaults. Changing one input at a time shows which assumptions move the break-even year. At a 6% rate, the payment falls to $1,918.56 and the break-even comes in year 8. Renting is still ahead by $5,977 after 7 years. At 5%, the payment is $1,717.83 and the break-even is year 5. Buying is then ahead by $20,214 after 7 years. At 4%, the payment is $1,527.73 and the break-even is year 4. Buying leads by $45,917 after 7 years. Higher rent also helps buying. At $2,600 rent, a price-to-rent ratio of 12.8, the break-even is year 7. At $2,800 rent, a ratio of 11.9, it is year 5. Home price growth of 5% a year moves the break-even to year 5. At 1% growth, buying never catches up within 30 years. The investment return works in the other direction, because the renter invests the $817 monthly difference. At a 3% return, the break-even is year 9. At 9%, buying never catches up within 30 years. A smaller down payment pushes the break-even out. With 10% down, or $40,000, the cash to buy drops to $52,000. The principal and interest payment is $2,472.95, mortgage insurance is added on top, and the break-even moves to year 30. You can size your own down payment with our down payment calculator , and see how a monthly investment grows with our compound interest calculator . These results come from a model. They are not measurements, and they are not a forecast of home prices, rents or returns. The default mortgage rate comes from the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey . It is the 30-year fixed-rate average for the week of October 22, 2026. That average was 7.32%, down from 7.40% the week before. The other defaults are planning assumptions, and you should replace them with local figures. Property tax is set at 1.0%, insurance at 0.5% and maintenance at 1.0% of the home's value a year. Closing costs are 3%, selling costs are 6%, and home prices and rent each grow 3% a year. The investment return is 6%, and renter's insurance is $15 a month. Property tax and insurance vary a lot by state, so enter your own tax rate and insurance quote. For rent, use what a similar home rents for near you, and our guide on how much to spend on rent can help you set that budget. The model leaves out the income-tax effects of owning. Mortgage interest and property tax deductions help only filers who itemize, so find your bracket with our tax bracket calculator before you count on them. Moving costs and special assessments are not modeled either. To set a home price you can carry, run our mortgage affordability calculator first. Based on our internal modeling, buy only if you expect to stay past the break-even year. At the defaults, the break-even is year 21, so a seven-year stay favors renting and investing the difference. A lower mortgage rate, higher rent or faster home price growth moves the break-even earlier. The result swings back toward renting if home prices stall or your invested cash earns more than assumed. If you expect to move within a few years, the defaults favor renting for any stay shorter than the break-even year, so keep renting and invest the cash. If you want to buy for space, stability or control of the property, the model does not price those reasons. This calculator is informational and is not financial advice. Enter your own price, rent and local tax rate in the rent vs buy calculator above, then read our renting vs buying guide for more on the decision. Frequently asked questions Is it better to rent or buy a house? It is better to buy only if you stay past the break-even year. At this calculator's defaults, that is year 21. For a 7-year stay, renting and investing comes out ahead by $41,156. Enter your own numbers above to find your break-even year. How long do you have to stay in a home for buying to beat renting? You need to stay past the break-even year, which this calculator finds for your inputs. At the defaults, it is year 21. A 5% mortgage rate or $2,800 rent moves it to year 5. At 1% home price growth, buying never catches up within 30 years. How does opportunity cost change the rent vs buy decision? Opportunity cost is the return your down payment and extra monthly costs would earn if you invested them instead. For the renter, the calculator invests the $92,000 of day-one cash and the $817 monthly difference at a 6% return. At a 3% return, the break-even moves to year 9. At 9%, buying never catches up within 30 years. What costs does a rent vs buy calculator include? This one counts the down payment and closing costs on day one, then the mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, maintenance, HOA dues and mortgage insurance. On the renting side, it counts rent, which grows each year, plus renter's insurance. It subtracts selling costs from the home's value when it figures buying net worth. It does not include moving costs, special assessments or income-tax effects. How much does the mortgage rate change the break-even year? At the default 7.32% rate, the break-even is year 21. At 6%, it moves to year 8. At 5%, it is year 5. At 4%, it is year 4. Does a bigger down payment make buying better? At the 7.32% default rate, which is above the 6% investment return, a bigger down payment helps buying. With 10% down, or $40,000, the cash to buy is $52,000. The principal and interest payment is $2,472.95, and mortgage insurance is added on top of that. The break-even moves to year 30, compared with year 21 at 20% down. What is a price-to-rent ratio? A price-to-rent ratio is the home price divided by 12 months of rent. At the defaults, it is 15.2. This calculator does not use a ratio cutoff to pick a winner. It runs the full model of costs, home equity and invested cash instead. Does this calculator include the mortgage interest tax deduction? No, the mortgage interest tax deduction is not modeled. That deduction, like the property tax deduction, helps only filers who itemize. You can find your bracket with our tax bracket calculator .
